questions.text: How long have you had a poor appetite, and are you eating significantly less than your normal intake?
questions.purpose: Characterise duration and severity of anorexia; >4 weeks requires systematic investigation
options: Less than 1 week — likely related to acute illness
Complete loss of appetite (not eating at all)

questions.text: Have you had significant unintentional weight loss alongside the reduced appetite?
questions.purpose: Weight loss with anorexia raises concern for underlying malignancy or serious systemic illness

questions.text: Do you have any abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or difficulty swallowing?
questions.purpose: GI symptoms with anorexia require GI investigation for peptic disease, obstruction, or malignancy

questions.text: Are you experiencing significant low mood, sadness, tearfulness, or loss of pleasure in life?
questions.purpose: Depression is one of the most common reversible causes of loss of appetite

questions.text: Do you have jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or dark urine suggesting liver disease?
questions.purpose: Hepatic or biliary disease commonly causes anorexia and nausea

questions.text: Have you had fever, night sweats, or other constitutional symptoms alongside the loss of appetite?
questions.purpose: Constitutional symptoms together with anorexia increase malignancy and serious infection likelihood

questions.text: Have you had any concerns about your body weight or image, or are you deliberately restricting food intake?
questions.purpose: Identify eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa which require specialist psychological assessment
